definition: Irreverence means playful, teasing lack of respect for what is usually taken seriously.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word irreverence. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know irreverence should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The tour guide's irreverence delighted the students: she introduced each solemn portrait by its sitter's childhood nickname.
Playfulness teases without any target at all — it stops short of irreverence, which pokes fun at something usually treated as serious.
Scorn goes further than irreverence: the irreverent joke still likes what it teases, while scorn holds its target in contempt.

Cheek is impudent boldness delivered live -- a saucy remark to a teacher or a boss, minor, face-to-face, and over in a moment. Irreverence targets institutions and solemn things rather than people, and can run through a whole book. A cheeky kid talks back; an irreverent columnist unsalutes the monument.

Mockery is ridicule meant to belittle -- the affection gone, the target meant to feel it. Irreverence teases what the room holds sacred and usually keeps a streak of liking for it. An irreverent biography can flatter its subject; mockery sets out to wound.

Flippancy is refusing to be serious when the moment asks for it -- a joke at the funeral, a shrug in the crisis. It is about mismatched tone, not about targets. Irreverence takes deliberate aim at something solemn; flippancy simply declines to rise to the occasion.

Every October the Grover Academy Bugle publishes its Founders' Week issue, and every October the headmaster braces himself.

The student editors take the school's most solemn traditions and tickle them: this year's issue ranked the oil portraits in the Great Hall by 'most likely to be judging you.' The paper's irreverence has rules the editors enforce on themselves -- no individual targets, no genuine wounds -- and underneath it runs an obvious fondness for the place.
Alumni collect the Founders' Week issues; two framed ones hang, of all places, in the headmaster's own study.
'They tease what they love,' he admits, 'and they only tease what everyone else salutes.'
